steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on few-shot relation extraction that uses images as extra evidence alongside the text. Motivate why visual information helps, explain the fusion challenges, describe our model at a high level, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Few-shot relation extraction and the two families of existing methods
- Problem: text-only methods fail when sentences lack context (Figure 1 example)
- Can visual information help? Challenges of multi-modal fusion
- Our model MFS-HVE: local and global visual features
- Multi-modal fusion unit (attention modules)
- Prototypes, hyperbolic distance, experiments
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - relation extraction: predict relation between two name entities in a sentence
  - few-shot learning: only a few labeled instances, less reliance on annotated data
  - category 1: plain text only, e.g. meta-learning prototypical networks (cite), siamese networks (cite)
  - category 2: external sources: relation information (cite), entity concepts (cite), side information (cite), external datasets (cite), graphs (cite)
- Problem
  - both explore single-modality text; performance drops when text lacks context
  - Figure 1: 'Dimitrie Popescu' + 'rower' -> relation 'sport' hard; word 'sport' not in text
  - uni-modal models wrongly extract 'winner' or 'candidate'
  - even knowledge graphs / similar words can't fix short sentences
- Question: can visual information supplement missing context?
  - image of person holding a trophy -> 'winner'
  - needs multi-modal learning; fusion is hard
  - (1) naive concatenation ignores semantics, may hurt (Sec. 4.4); background faces = noise
  - (2) existing multi-modal models (Sec. 2.2) fuse global features only, ignore visual objects ('person', 'boat')
- MFS-HVE (Multimodal Few-Shot model based on Hybrid Visual Evidence)
  - textual feature extractor (Sec. 3.2.1), visual feature extractor (Sec. 3.2.2)
  - local, low resolution (Sec. 3.3.2): embedding of detected objects
  - global, high resolution (Sec. 3.3.1): embedding of whole image
  - local = sparse; global = more info but noise -> combine both
- Fusion unit, inspired by cross-modal attention (cite)
  - image-guided attention, scaled dot-product (cite): global image features + text
  - object-guided attention: detected objects + name entities
  - hybrid feature attention: fuses all, weight vector multiplied by multi-modal representations
- Prediction and experiments
  - concatenate text / image-guided / object-guided features via cross-modality encoder
  - prototypical networks (cite): relation representation; mean of support vectors as prototype (cite)
  - hierarchical structure of objects and entities (Sec. 3.3.3) -> hyperbolic distance
  - datasets MNRE (cite), FewRel (cite); FewRel text only -> crawl images with icrawler (Sec. 4.1)
  - multi-modal beats text-only; ablation and parameter sensitivity studies
- Contributions
  - first approach for multi-modal few-shot relation extraction
  - three attentions integrate visual and textual semantics
  - experiments on two public datasets: visual info supplements missing context

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Relation extraction is the task of predicting the relation between two name entities in a sentence. Few-shot learning has drawn more attention to reduce the reliance on high-quality annotated data, since it only needs a few labeled instances for training to adapt to new tasks. Existing few-shot relation extraction methods can roughly be divided into two categories. The first category only uses plain text data and no auxiliary information. For example, meta-learning models like prototypical networks and siamese neural networks are trained with only a few examples for each class to extract relations. The second category brings in external data sources to make up for the limited information in those methods and improve few-shot relation extraction, such as relation information, concepts of entities, side information, external datasets, and graphs.

However, these methods mostly work with single-modality text data, and their performance can drop a lot when the text lacks context. For example, in Figure 1, there are two name entities ‘Dimitrie Popescu’ and ‘rower’, and it is hard for text-based models to detect the relation ‘sport’ without other supplementary information, because the word ‘sport’ or similar words do not appear in the text. So uni-modal models will wrongly extract the relation ‘winner’ or ‘candidate’ for the two name entities based on the short textual sentence. Even models that use external information like knowledge graphs or related words with similar meanings still can not extract the relation correctly, because the given textual sentences are short and have limited information.

So we ask: can visual information be a good external source to supplement the missing contexts in textual sentences for few-shot relation extraction? In the case above, we can easily classify the relation into ‘winner’ with the guidance of an image that shows a person holding a trophy. Using visual information to support contextual information for texts involves multi-modal learning. However, fusing information from different modalities is a challenging task too. First, just concatenating textual and visual features without considering semantic information may even hurt the performance, as shown in Sec. 4.4. For example, in Figure 1, the faces of multiple people in the background are noise for the image with the relation ‘sport’. Second, existing multi-modal models (Sec. 2.2) mainly fuse global visual features with text and do not consider the semantic information of visual objects in images. In Figure 1, visual objects such as ‘person’ and ‘boat’ contain information that is essential to the relation ‘sport’.

- MFS-HVE (Multimodal Few-Shot model based on Hybrid Visual Evidence)
  - textual feature extractor (Sec. 3.2.1), visual feature extractor (Sec. 3.2.2)
  - local low resolution (Sec. 3.3.2) = detected objects; global high resolution (Sec. 3.3.1) = whole image
  - local sparse, global noisy -> combine both
- Fusion unit, inspired by cross-modal attention
  - image-guided attention (scaled dot-product): global image + text
  - object-guided attention: objects + name entities
  - hybrid feature attention: weight vector multiplied by multi-modal representations
- Prediction and experiments
  - cross-modality encoder concatenates the three feature types
  - prototypical networks: mean of support vectors as prototype
  - hierarchical structure (Sec. 3.3.3) -> hyperbolic distance
  - MNRE, FewRel; crawl images with icrawler for FewRel (Sec. 4.1)
  - multi-modal beats text-only; ablation + parameter sensitivity
- Contributions
  - first multi-modal few-shot relation extraction approach
  - three attentions integrate visual and textual semantics
  - experiments on two datasets: visual info supplements missing context

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Relation extraction is the task of predicting the relation between two name entities in a sentence. Few-shot learning has drawn more attention to reduce the reliance on high-quality annotated data, since it only needs a few labeled instances for training to adapt to new tasks. Existing few-shot relation extraction methods can roughly be divided into two categories. The first category only uses plain text data and no auxiliary information. For example, meta-learning models like prototypical networks and siamese neural networks are trained with only a few examples for each class to extract relations. The second category brings in external data sources to make up for the limited information in those methods and improve few-shot relation extraction, such as relation information, concepts of entities, side information, external datasets, and graphs.

However, these methods mostly work with single-modality text data, and their performance can drop a lot when the text lacks context. For example, in Figure 1, there are two name entities ‘Dimitrie Popescu’ and ‘rower’, and it is hard for text-based models to detect the relation ‘sport’ without other supplementary information, because the word ‘sport’ or similar words do not appear in the text. So uni-modal models will wrongly extract the relation ‘winner’ or ‘candidate’ for the two name entities based on the short textual sentence. Even models that use external information like knowledge graphs or related words with similar meanings still can not extract the relation correctly, because the given textual sentences are short and have limited information.

So we ask: can visual information be a good external source to supplement the missing contexts in textual sentences for few-shot relation extraction? In the case above, we can easily classify the relation into ‘winner’ with the guidance of an image that shows a person holding a trophy. Using visual information to support contextual information for texts involves multi-modal learning. However, fusing information from different modalities is a challenging task too. First, just concatenating textual and visual features without considering semantic information may even hurt the performance, as shown in Sec. 4.4. For example, in Figure 1, the faces of multiple people in the background are noise for the image with the relation ‘sport’. Second, existing multi-modal models (Sec. 2.2) mainly fuse global visual features with text and do not consider the semantic information of visual objects in images. In Figure 1, visual objects such as ‘person’ and ‘boat’ contain information that is essential to the relation ‘sport’.

To address these challenges, we propose a Multimodal Few-Shot model based on Hybrid Visual Evidence (MFS-HVE) for relation extraction. First we generate the representations with the textual feature extractor in Sec. 3.2.1 and the visual feature extractor in Sec. 3.2.2. We look at the visual representations from both a local perspective in low resolution (Sec. 3.3.2) and a global perspective in high resolution (Sec. 3.3.1). A local feature vector is the embedding of the objects detected from the image, and a global feature vector is the embedding of the whole image. Local features only focus on objects, so global features can overcome the sparsity problem with more information, but they may contain noise (irrelevant information). We integrate both local features and global features to solve both the sparsity problem and the noise problem.

Secondly, we propose a multi-modal fusion unit that is inspired by the cross-modal attention mechanism. It includes image-guided attention, object-guided attention, and hybrid feature attention to integrate semantic information from different modalities at both the global and the local levels. From the global perspective, image-guided attention is based on the scaled dot-product attention and combines global feature vectors from the image with texts to capture the semantic interaction between visual regions of images and texts. From the local perspective, object-guided attention fuses objects detected from the image with relevant name entities from the textual sentences. Then the hybrid feature attention fuses all the textual and visual information, including global image features and local object features. The hybrid feature attention generates a weight vector, which is multiplied by the multi-modal representations.

Finally, we concatenate text features, image-guided features, and object-guided features through a cross-modality encoder to get the final multi-modal representations. Each relation representation is calculated based on the prototypical networks. Based on the prototypical networks, we compute the mean value of all multi-modal support vectors as the prototype for each relation. Because the detected objects and name entities have a hierarchical structure, which is discussed in Sec. 3.3.3, we calculate hyperbolic distance between multi-modal query representations and prototypes to predict the relation. We do extensive experiments on two public datasets, MNRE and FewRel, to evaluate whether semantic visual information can supplement the missing contexts in textual sentences for few-shot relation extraction. FewRel is a uni-modal dataset that only contains text, so we crawl an image automatically with icrawler for each instance to provide visual information, which can help future research on multi-modal few-shot relation extraction. The details are in Sec. 4.1. We compare MFS-HVE with some state-of-the-art uni-modal few-shot relation extraction models and some multi-modal fusion methods with the same feature extractors, and we show that in general models with multi-modal information perform better than text-only models. We also do ablation studies and parameter sensitivity studies to learn the impact of each attention and function. The contributions of this paper are:

- We propose the first approach (MFS-HVE) for multi-modal few-shot relation extraction. Existing few-shot relation extraction models only focus on one data modality.

- MFS-HVE combines information from different modalities with image-guided attention, object-guided attention, and hybrid feature attention to integrate semantic visual information and textual information.

- We do extensive experiments on two public datasets. The results show that adding visual information can supplement the missing contexts in textual sentences for the few-shot relation extraction task.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Relation extraction aims to predict the relation between two name entities in a sentence. To alleviate the reliance on high-quality annotated data, few-shot learning has drawn more attention, as it requires only a few labeled instances for training to adapt to new tasks. Existing few-shot relation extraction methods can be roughly divided into two categories. One category uses only plain text data, without any auxiliary information. For example, meta-learning models such as prototypical networks [1] and siamese neural networks [2] are trained with only a few examples for each class to extract relations. The other category introduces external data sources such as relation information [3,4], concepts of entities [5], side information [6], external datasets [7], and graphs [8] to compensate for the limited information in the above methods and enhance performance in few-shot relation extraction.

However, these methods mainly explore single-modality text-based data and may suffer a significant performance decline when texts lack context. For example, in Figure 1, given two name entities ‘Dimitrie Popescu’ and ‘rower’, it is difficult for text-based models to detect the relation ‘sport’ without other supplementary information, because the word ‘sport’ or similar words do not appear in the text. As a result, uni-modal models will incorrectly extract the relation ‘winner’ or ‘candidate’ for the two name entities based on the short textual sentence. Even models using external information such as knowledge graphs or related words with similar meanings still cannot correctly extract the relation, due to the limited information in short textual sentences.

Therefore, we ask: can visual information be a good external source to supplement the missing contexts in textual sentences for few-shot relation extraction? In the above case, we can easily classify the relation into ‘winner’ with the guidance of an image showing a person holding a trophy. Utilizing visual information to support contextual information for texts involves multi-modal learning. However, fusing information from different modalities is itself a challenging task. First, simply concatenating textual and visual features without considering semantic information may even have a negative impact on performance, as shown in Sec. 4.4. For example, in Figure 1, the multiple people’s faces in the background are noise for the image with the relation ‘sport’. Second, existing multi-modal models (Sec. 2.2) mainly focus on fusing global visual features with text, without considering the semantic information of visual objects in images. In Figure 1, visual objects such as ‘person’ and ‘boat’ contain essential information for the relation ‘sport’.

To address these challenges, we propose a Multimodal Few-Shot model based on Hybrid Visual Evidence (MFS-HVE) for relation extraction. We first generate the representations through the textual feature extractor in Sec. 3.2.1 and the visual feature extractor in Sec. 3.2.2. We consider the visual representations from both the local perspective in low resolution (Sec. 3.3.2) and the global perspective in high resolution (Sec. 3.3.1). More specifically, a local feature vector is the embedding of the objects detected in the image, and a global feature vector is the embedding of the whole image. Because local features only focus on objects, global features can overcome the problem of sparsity with more information; however, they may contain noise (irrelevant information). Secondly, inspired by the cross-modal attention mechanism [9], we propose a multi-modal fusion unit including image-guided attention, object-guided attention, and hybrid feature attention to integrate semantic information from different modalities at both global and local levels. From the global perspective, image-guided attention based on scaled dot-product attention [10] combines global feature vectors from the image with texts to capture the semantic interaction between visual regions of images and texts. From the local perspective, object-guided attention fuses objects detected in the image with relevant name entities from the textual sentences. The hybrid feature attention then fuses all textual and visual information, including global image features and local object features, and generates a weight vector that is multiplied by the multi-modal representations.

Finally, we concatenate text features, image-guided features, and object-guided features through a cross-modality encoder to generate the final multi-modal representations. Each relation representation is calculated based on the prototypical networks [11]: based on the prototypical networks [11], we compute the mean value of all multi-modal support vectors as the prototype representing each relation. Because of the hierarchical structure of the detected objects and name entities discussed in Sec. 3.3.3, hyperbolic distance is calculated between multi-modal query representations and prototypes to predict the relation. Since FewRel is a uni-modal dataset containing only text, we automatically crawl an image with icrawler for each instance to provide visual information, which can facilitate future research on multi-modal few-shot relation extraction. Details are given in Sec. 4.1. By comparing MFS-HVE with state-of-the-art uni-modal few-shot relation extraction models and multi-modal fusion methods with the same feature extractors, we show that, in general, models with multi-modal information perform better than text-only models. We also conduct ablation studies and parameter sensitivity studies to learn the impact of each attention and function. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as:

- We propose the first approach (MFS-HVE) for multi-modal few-shot relation extraction. Existing models for few-shot relation extraction focus only on a single data modality.

- MFS-HVE combines information from different modalities through image-guided attention, object-guided attention, and hybrid feature attention to integrate semantic visual information and textual information.

- We conduct extensive experiments on two public datasets. The results show that introducing visual information can supplement the missing contexts in textual sentences for the few-shot relation extraction task.
